newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory cocoa arrivals reach 920-960,000 T - industry.
newsitem.headline: Ivory cocoa arrivals reach 920-960,000 T - industry.

text.p: Cocoa arrivals recorded at Ivory Coast's ports were in a 920-960,000 tonnes range by March 7, compared with 940,000 in the record 1995/96 season, industry sources and crop analysts said.
"The cocoa is there, unfortunately, so this year is not too different from last year," said one source.
Ivory Coast produced a record 1.2 million tonnes of cocoa in 1995/96 (Oct-Sept) after an unprecedented one million tonne main crop and a larger than expected 200,000 tonne mid-crop (April-Sept).
Exporters disagreed on latest arrivals figures but local crop analysts said they expected 1996/97 main crop (Oct-March) totals by the end of March to be close to 1995/96 levels.
Ivory Coast forecast a total crop of 950,000 tonnes for 1996/97 but commodities minister Guy-Alain Gauze said this week that it had now sold 800,000 tonnes of cocoa and had no more to sell.
Exporters said at least 870,000 tonnes of exportable cocoa had been declared by early March.
Another 60,000 tonnes or more of lower grade beans would most likely be mixed in with higher grades to reach export standards.
Quality inspectors said average bean sizes this week had started to slip from 95-100 beans per 100 grams. Bean sizes from some regions were edging down towards 120 per 100 grams.
"Humidity is less than eight percent," said one inspector.
Ivory Coast's bean export standard is 105 beans per 100 grams with less than eight percent bean humidity.
The shape of the approaching mid-crop harvest is expected to be clearer as pod counters complete their work later this month.
The cumulative arrivals data dates back to October 1 although Ivory Coast opened its 1996/97 season on October 24, around three weeks later than usual.
